opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think chess is actually a really revealing test case, precisely because the rules are so clear. Chess is a closed world. There are maybe a dozen rules that matter, they're written down in thousands of places on the internet, and GPT-4 has certainly seen them, and seen millions of games besides. So if these systems truly understood what they were reading, chess should be the easiest thing in the world for them, at least at the level of playing legal moves.

And what you see instead is that it can play a pretty plausible opening, because openings are heavily represented in the training data. It's basically regurgitating sequences it has seen many times. But once you get out of book, into the middlegame, into positions it hasn't seen, things start to fall apart. It makes illegal moves. It moves a bishop like a knight, it forgets where pieces are, it resurrects captured pieces. And that tells you something important: it doesn't have a stable internal model of the board. It's not tracking the state of the world; it's predicting what text tends to come next in something that looks like a chess transcript.

Now, people will say, "But it's better than it used to be," or "With the right prompting it gets to some decent rating." Fine. But think about what that means. A fifty-year-old chess program running on a calculator never makes an illegal move, because it actually represents the rules and the board. A seven-year-old child who's been taught the rules for twenty minutes doesn't move a rook diagonally. So the failure isn't about lacking enough data or enough parameters. It's about the architecture. These systems are fantastic at mimicry and pretty weak at abstraction, at extracting a rule and applying it reliably to new cases.

And that's my broader concern. Chess is a toy, but the same issue shows up everywhere: in arithmetic, in reasoning about time and space, in keeping facts straight over a long conversation. If you can't reliably follow the rules of chess after reading them a million times, why would I trust you to reliably follow the rules of medicine or law or a company's financial policies? To me it's another piece of evidence that we need hybrid approaches, systems that combine the pattern recognition of neural networks with explicit symbolic representations of knowledge and rules. Pure scaling isn't going to get you there on its own.

r001.rationale: It contrasts GPT-4’s illegal moves with a fifty-year-old chess program that never makes one, challenging claims that GPT-4’s chess performance is impressive.

r002.rationale: It calls GPT-4’s play mimicry and describes predicting likely transcript text, but does not contrast that with or explicitly characterize it as not using tree search.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's a perfect illustration of the point I've been making for years, honestly. If you look at the games people have posted, GPT-4 can rattle off opening theory beautifully, because it's seen millions of games in its training data. The Ruy Lopez, the Sicilian, whatever, it's all memorized. But then you get into the middlegame, and once the position drifts away from anything it's seen before, it starts making illegal moves. It'll move a bishop through a pawn. It'll castle after the king has already moved. It'll resurrect a piece that was captured three moves ago.

And that tells you something really fundamental. It doesn't have a model of the board. It doesn't actually know where the pieces are. What it has is a statistical approximation of what chess notation tends to look like, and that approximation is good enough to fool you for the first fifteen moves. People see that and say, "Look, it plays chess!" No. A system that plays chess doesn't make illegal moves. A five-year-old who's been taught the rules doesn't make illegal moves, or at least if they do, you can correct them once and they stop.

What's striking to me is that we solved chess, in a real sense, decades ago. Deep Blue beat Kasparov in 1997. Stockfish runs on your phone and would crush any human alive. Those systems have explicit representations: here is the board, here are the legal moves, here is a search over the tree. They're reliable in a way that a large language model simply is not. So we've gone from systems that genuinely play chess to a system that sort of pantomimes playing chess, and somehow that's being celebrated as progress toward general intelligence.

Now, the obvious response is, "Well, just hook it up to a chess engine," and sure, you can do that. But notice what you've conceded at that point. You've conceded that the neural network can't do the thing on its own, and that you need a symbolic component with an explicit world model to get reliability. That's neurosymbolic AI. That's what I've been arguing for since the nineties. The interesting question isn't whether GPT-4 can play chess. It's why anyone expected it to, given that it has no mechanism for tracking state, and what that tells you about all the other domains where we're trusting these things to reason about the world.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts GPT-4’s illegal moves with the reliability of Deep Blue and Stockfish, then calls celebrating its performance misplaced.

r002.rationale: It describes GPT-4 as “pantomim[ing]” chess through statistical patterns and contrasts that with chess engines’ explicit search over a game tree.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think we have to distinguish between producing plausible chess moves and reliably playing chess. Those are different achievements. A language model can learn a great deal from records of games—openings, common sequences, even patterns that look quite sophisticated. But the crucial question is whether it consistently tracks the board and respects the rules when the game takes an unfamiliar turn.

I wouldn’t dismiss good moves as meaningless. Learning those patterns is impressive. But I’d want systematic tests: Does it make illegal moves? Can it handle unusual positions? Does it recognize when its own move leaves its king in check? A few impressive examples don’t settle those questions.

Chess is useful here because the rules are explicit. We can distinguish fluency from correctness. And that’s the broader issue with these systems: how do we turn something that often produces a convincing answer into something we can reliably trust?

r001.rationale: It questions GPT-4’s reliability and asks whether it makes illegal moves, but does not mention older chess software or use its avoidance of illegal moves to challenge excitement.

r002.rationale: It says a language model can learn patterns from game records, but does not characterize GPT-4’s chess play as mimicry or contrast it with tree search.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d distinguish between producing moves that look plausible and reliably playing legal, coherent chess. Those are different achievements. A language model might reproduce familiar openings from patterns in its training data, but the interesting question is whether it consistently tracks the board: where the pieces are, what moves are legal, and how each move changes the position.

If GPT-4 does that reliably, that’s interesting evidence of competence. If it loses track and makes illegal moves, that tells us something about the limits of that competence. I wouldn’t infer a robust understanding of chess from a few impressive sequences. I’d want systematic tests, including unfamiliar positions, and a clear distinction between the model playing on its own and the model using a chess engine.
